passage:
Wednesday night
Skipped lunch again to finish the audit summary. Mid-afternoon I opened Gurleen's comments on my draft and every line felt like an attack. I typed a reply in capitals, "If the brief had been read properly...", and nearly hit send. Then I just sat there thinking: I'm terrible at this job, I'll never get promoted, why did I even take it? All that, on an ordinary Wednesday. Someone brought samosas round the floor. I ate one without tasting it, then another. Afterwards I read Gurleen's comments again. They were fair. Helpful, even; she'd said she liked my structure. Deleted the email and wrote, "Thanks, will fix by tomorrow." Note to self: the job didn't get worse this afternoon. I was just running on empty.
Indu

qa.q: What did Indu skip to finish the audit summary?
qa.a: Lunch.

qa.q: How did Indu feel about the job before eating?
qa.a: Indu felt hopeless and defensive, sure of being terrible at the job and never getting promoted.

qa.q: What did Indu do after eating, and what could help next time?
qa.a: Indu reread the comments, deleted the angry email and replied calmly; next time, eating before opening feedback could stop the spiral.

qa.q: What would have changed for Gurleen if the angry email had gone out?
qa.a: Gurleen would have been hurt by a sharp reply to fair, helpful comments, and the working relationship would have taken a knock.

grounding: Shows a busy professional who skipped lunch nearly sending a harsh email and feeling hopeless, until eating shrinks the problem back to size.

passage:
Kishore: this project is a disaster. i think i'm just bad at my job
Siddharth: whoa. what happened?
Kishore: client moved the deadline up. been fixing the deck since morning. also snapped at the intern for asking where the stapler was
Siddharth: since morning?? did you eat lunch
Kishore: no time
Siddharth: it's nearly evening. you're not bad at your job, you're running on nothing
Kishore: that's not it. everything is just falling apart
Siddharth: humour me. go downstairs, get poha from the cart, then look at the deck again
Kishore: fine
(later)
Kishore: ok. the deck is mostly done actually. only two slides left
Kishore: and i said sorry to the intern
Siddharth: good. proud of you
Kishore: why does everything look like the end of the world when i'm hungry

qa.q: What did Kishore snap at the intern about?
qa.a: Asking where the stapler was.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling before going downstairs?
qa.a: Kishore felt hopeless and overwhelmed, sure that everything was falling apart.

qa.q: What small step helped, and why?
qa.a: Getting poha from the cart before looking at the deck again; with food inside, the problem looked smaller and Kishore could apologise to the intern.

qa.q: How does Siddharth read Kishore's panic?
qa.a: Siddharth sees hunger, not failure, and gently pushes for food before any big conclusions.

grounding: Illustrates a professional working through lunch who snaps at someone and feels hopeless about work, until food makes the problem look smaller.

passage:
Amandeep: can we talk about the wedding budget tonight? my parents called again
Dolma: yes, but not right now
Dolma: i just heard my own voice on that call and it was sharp. haven't eaten since breakfast
Amandeep: ah. the danger zone
Dolma: exactly. if we start now i'll say something about your parents that i don't mean
Dolma: after dinner? i'll pick up dal and rotis on the way home
Amandeep: deal. i'll put the kettle on
(after dinner)
Dolma: ok, fed and human again
Dolma: also sorry i was short with you on the phone earlier. that wasn't fair, hungry or not
Amandeep: thanks for saying that. budget now?
Dolma: now. i'll get the notebook
Amandeep: and i'll get the calculator. no wedding without a spreadsheet

qa.q: What does Dolma pick up on the way home?
qa.a: Dal and rotis.

qa.q: What was Dolma worried about if they talked right away?
qa.a: Dolma worried about saying something unfair about Amandeep's parents, because hunger had already made that voice sharp.

qa.q: What makes Dolma's approach mature?
qa.a: Dolma notices the edge, eats first and delays the hard talk, and then still apologises for the sharp tone instead of blaming hunger.

qa.q: How might Amandeep feel about the delay?
qa.a: Amandeep seems relieved and understanding, glad to wait for a calmer talk and to hear the apology.

grounding: Shows someone hearing the edge in their own voice, eating before a hard conversation and still owning the earlier rudeness afterwards.

passage: The last customer left Payal's tailoring shop in Sehore at dusk, and Usha, her sister-in-law and partner, spread the order book on the counter. "We need to talk about the school uniforms. You promised them for Friday without asking me." Payal felt "You always..." rising in her throat, heard the edge in her own voice and stopped. She hadn't eaten since the morning roti; a wedding blouse had swallowed her lunch hour. "Usha, give me a little time. I'm starving, and I'll say it badly." She walked to the tea stall, ate a plate of poha and came back. "Sorry I snapped when you asked about the thread earlier. That was rude, hungry or not. Now, Friday. You're right, I should have asked." They split the uniforms between them and wrote the plan in the book.

qa.q: What had Payal promised for Friday?
qa.a: The school uniforms.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when Usha raised the order?
qa.a: She felt irritation rising, heard the edge in her own voice and realised hunger was part of it.

qa.q: What did Payal do after eating that mattered, and why?
qa.a: She apologised for snapping earlier and admitted she should have asked, so eating first did not become an excuse for rudeness.

qa.q: What would change for Usha if Payal had argued on an empty stomach?
qa.a: Usha would likely have heard "You always..." instead of an apology, and the uniform order would have turned into a fight.

grounding: Illustrates a person noticing the edge in her voice, eating before a hard talk, and still apologising for earlier rudeness once steady.

passage:
"Ammi, up! Up!" Irfan tugged at Afreen's dupatta, whining.
"Beta, I'm cooking. Go play with your truck."
"No truck!" He flopped against her legs, cheeks flushed.
Abbu came in from the heat. "He's been cranky since the bazaar. Sleepy too."
"It's this weather," Afreen said. Then she stopped. "When did he last drink?"
Abbu filled the little steel cup. Irfan gulped it down and held it out. "More!"
"If he stays droopy, we'll ring the doctor," Abbu said.

qa.q: Where had Irfan been before he got cranky?
qa.a: The bazaar.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling when he tugged at Afreen's dupatta?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and needy but could not say he was thirsty, so he whined and clung.

qa.q: What simple step helped, and what could the family do on the next hot day?
qa.a: Giving him water; on hot, busy days they could offer his cup regularly instead of waiting for the fussing.

qa.q: How did Afreen explain the whining at first?
qa.a: She put it down to the weather, until she stopped and wondered when he had last had a drink.

grounding: Shows a toddler who has not had enough to drink on a hot day turning fussy, clingy and sleepy, and a cup of water as the forgotten rescue.

passage: Note to Manoj's parents, Thursday. Our garden walk ran long in the heat, and I realised later that Manoj had barely touched his bottle. By noon he was fussy, rubbing his face, wanting to be carried and nodding off on my lap. He couldn't tell us he was thirsty. I gave him small sips in the shade, and he perked up, asking "more, more". From now on we will offer every child water regularly on hot days. Sabina

qa.q: What did Manoj ask for after the sips?
qa.a: "More, more."

qa.q: Why was Manoj fussy and clingy by noon?
qa.a: He was thirsty and uncomfortable in the heat but could not say so, so he felt miserable and wanted comfort.

qa.q: What did Sabina change, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Offering every child water regularly on hot days, because toddlers cannot ask for it and adults easily forget.

qa.q: How might Manoj's parents feel reading the note?
qa.a: They may feel reassured that Sabina noticed and acted, and reminded to keep offering water at home.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler who drank too little on a hot outing becoming fussy, sleepy and clingy, and regular water offered as a simple fix.

passage:
Monday: Pema played football through the whole break in the blazing sun. Her water bottle stayed full in her bag. By maths her head throbbed, and when Samir borrowed her ruler she snapped, "Just take it!" and put her head on the desk. At home Mummy asked, "Did you drink anything today?" Pema thought hard. "Umm. No."
Wednesday: Pema made a rule: a sip at every whistle. Samir laughed, then copied her.
Friday: After a hard match, Pema noticed her mouth was dry and a small ache was starting behind her eyes. She drank before anyone reminded her. In maths she was cheerful, and she even lent Samir her ruler without being asked.

qa.q: What rule did Pema make on Wednesday?
qa.a: A sip at every whistle.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling in maths on Monday?
qa.a: She felt achy, tired and grumpy, which is why she snapped at Samir.

qa.q: What changed by Friday, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Pema noticed her dry mouth and the starting ache and drank without a reminder, so she is learning to read her own body.

qa.q: How might Samir have felt when Pema snapped on Monday?
qa.a: Samir was probably surprised or a bit hurt, not knowing that Pema was thirsty and headachy.

grounding: Shows a child who forgets to drink while playing hard in the sun feeling headachy and grumpy, then learning to notice thirst and carry a bottle.

passage: Tarun, when your Dida was your age in Kolkata, I, Bidisha, played kho-kho in the school yard till my plaits were soaked. I never drank a drop; water was for babies, I thought. One April afternoon I came back to class with a pounding head and legs like wet rope. I shouted at my best friend Mitali for humming, then cried over a spelling test. Our games teacher, Mrs Ghosh, looked at my cracked lips and sat me under the neem tree with her own tin mug of water. "Your body was asking, and you weren't listening," she said. Next morning I carried a brass bottle to school, and I have carried one ever since.

qa.q: Where did Mrs Ghosh sit Bidisha?
qa.a: Under the neem tree.

qa.q: What was young Bidisha feeling back in class that afternoon?
qa.a: She felt achy, drained and irritable, so she shouted at Mitali and then cried over a spelling test.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Bidisha's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Mrs Ghosh noticing the cracked lips and giving her water; it taught Bidisha to listen to thirst, and she began carrying a bottle.

qa.q: How might Mitali have felt when Bidisha shouted about the humming?
qa.a: Mitali was probably hurt and puzzled, since the humming was harmless and the anger came from Bidisha's thirst.

grounding: Illustrates a child playing hard in the sun without drinking becoming headachy and grumpy, then learning to notice thirst and carry a bottle.

subtype: Sports practice fatigue and short temper [Observer]
passage: Shreya, now that you're coaching, let me, Sharmila, tell you about Harpreet. The children called me Sharmila Ma'am. Harpreet was fifteen, always first to warm-up, always laughing. One hot May week she changed. She jogged at the back, dragged her feet in the relays and snapped at a teammate who only asked for the baton. I had a whole speech ready about attitude and effort. Then I saw her bottle lying empty since morning, her face flushed and blotchy. I sat her in the shade with water and let her rest out the next drill. That week I added water breaks between every drill for the whole squad. Harpreet was laughing again by Friday. No pep talk of mine ever did what that water jug did.

qa.q: What did Harpreet snap at a teammate about?
qa.a: The teammate only asked for the baton.

qa.q: What was Sharmila tempted to do, and how did she feel?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and was ready with a speech about attitude and effort, before she noticed the empty bottle.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Sharmila's story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Choosing water and rest in the shade over a lecture, then adding water breaks for everyone; it fixed the body's need behind the mood.

qa.q: How might that week have felt for Harpreet?
qa.a: Probably draining and confusing; she was hot and dried out, so running felt heavy and small requests made her snap.

grounding: Shows a coach noticing a usually keen teen turn slow and sharp after training in heat without drinking, and water breaks helping more than a pep talk.

subtype: Sports practice fatigue and short temper [Observer]
passage: The district kho-kho trials were three days away, the heat was brutal, and the ground's tap had run dry. Coach Uday watched Manjula, sixteen and usually the loudest in the team, trudge through her chases. When a teammate tagged her out, she threw her cap and muttered, "What's the point?" Uday felt his temper rise; he had no time for sulks this week. Then he saw her lips, dry and pale, and remembered the empty tap. He blew the whistle, sent two players to the shop with money from his own wallet and made everyone sit in the shade and drink. Manjula drank a whole bottle in silence. After a short rest she was back, laughing at her own clumsy fall.

qa.q: Why was there no water at the ground?
qa.a: The ground's tap had run dry.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when Manjula threw her cap?
qa.a: He felt his temper rise under the pressure of the trials, before he noticed her dry, pale lips.

qa.q: What did Uday choose, and why was it better than a scolding?
qa.a: He stopped practice for water and rest in the shade, which dealt with the heat and thirst behind the mood instead of the mood itself.

qa.q: What was the practice like for Manjula before the break?
qa.a: She was probably exhausted and dried out, so every chase felt pointless and a small loss made her snap.

grounding: Illustrates a coach under time pressure seeing a keen teen turn slow and moody in the heat and choosing water and rest over a pep talk.

subtype: Mistaking thirst for tiredness or hunger [Actor]
passage: Tenzin, you keep reaching for tea at three and then yawning at your desk. When I, Hemant, was twenty and at college in Pune, I did the same. Every afternoon I felt heavy and foggy. I'd buy tea and a packet of biscuits, then another, and still read the same page four times. I thought I was just lazy, or hungry. One day my hostel neighbour Ravi tossed me his water bottle and said, "Drink this before the next tea." I finished half of it, walked once round the building and sat down again. The fog didn't vanish every time, but that day the page finally made sense. I started keeping a bottle on my desk after that.

qa.q: What did Ravi toss to Hemant?
qa.a: His water bottle.

qa.q: How did young Hemant feel about the foggy afternoons?
qa.a: Hemant felt heavy and frustrated, blaming laziness or guessing it was hunger.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Hemant's story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Drinking water and taking a short walk before the next tea; it sometimes cleared the fog that tea and biscuits had not.

qa.q: How might Ravi have seen Hemant's afternoons?
qa.a: Ravi probably noticed a neighbour living on tea and biscuits and guessed that water was the missing piece.

grounding: Shows a young adult reaching for tea and snacks when the body wants water, feeling foggy all afternoon, and water with a short break sometimes clearing it.

subtype: Mistaking thirst for tiredness or hunger [Actor]
passage: The library fans had broken, exams were a week away, and Tenzin had only a few coins left for the month. By afternoon he was slumped over his notes, eyes drifting. He counted out enough for another chai and a packet of chips, telling himself he needed fuel. It didn't help; the words still swam. Across the table, Eshaan slid a steel bottle over. "When did you last drink water, not chai?" Tenzin couldn't remember. He drank slowly, splashed his face at the tap and walked down the corridor and back. When he sat again, his head felt a little clearer. "Cheaper than chips," Eshaan whispered. Tenzin grinned and kept the coins.

qa.q: What did Eshaan slide across the table?
qa.a: A steel bottle.

qa.q: How was Tenzin feeling when he reached for chai and chips?
qa.a: He felt drained and worried, with exams a week away and few coins left, and thought he needed fuel without realising he was thirsty.

qa.q: What helped, and why is it worth trying again?
qa.a: Drinking water, splashing his face and a short walk; it cleared his head a little and cost nothing.

qa.q: How does Eshaan see Tenzin's slump?
qa.a: Eshaan suspects thirst rather than hunger or laziness, and offers water with a quiet question instead of a lecture.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult short of money and focus reaching for chai and snacks when the body wants water, and a drink plus a short break clearing the fog.

passage:
"You look like the ceiling fell on you," Vishal said at the office pantry.
Joseph pressed his temples. "Headache. Again. This job is draining the life out of me."
"What have you had today?"
"Coffee at nine, tea at eleven, tea after lunch, another coffee now."
"And water?"
Joseph blinked. "Does the water in the tea count?"
"Not really. When I lived on tea, I got the same headaches and snapped at everyone. I started keeping a bottle on my desk."
"You think that's it? Not the job?"
"Maybe both. Try it this week and see."
Joseph filled a bottle at the cooler. "If the headaches keep coming, I'll check with a doctor too."
"Good plan."

qa.q: Where were Joseph and Vishal talking?
qa.a: At the office pantry.

qa.q: What did Joseph believe was causing the headaches, and how did he feel about it?
qa.a: He blamed the job and felt drained and fed up, as if it was taking the life out of him.

qa.q: Which choice is sensible here, and why?
qa.a: Keeping water on the desk this week while seeing a doctor if the headaches keep coming, because it tests a simple cause without ignoring a real one.

qa.q: How does Vishal see Joseph's complaint?
qa.a: Vishal recognises the pattern from living on tea and gently suggests water, without dismissing that the job may also be hard.

grounding: Shows a desk worker living on tea and coffee who ends the day with headaches and blames the job, and a colleague suggesting regular water.

passage:
Last spring I was sure I had chosen the wrong career. Every evening I left the design studio with a thudding head, snapped at my flatmate Hansa over the dishes and lay on the sofa feeling flat. I blamed the clients, the deadlines, the whole industry. I even opened a job site one night. Then Hansa, who puts up with a lot, asked what I drank at work. Masala chai, coffee, more chai. Water? I honestly couldn't remember. She handed me her old blue bottle and said, "Fill it twice before you blame your boss." I felt silly, but I tried it. The headaches eased and the evenings stopped feeling so grey. Hansa also said that if the headaches kept coming, I should see a doctor; they didn't. I still work in design. I still drink chai. But the blue bottle sits by my keyboard.
Dilnaz

qa.q: What did Hansa hand Dilnaz?
qa.a: Her old blue bottle.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel about the career before trying the bottle?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt flat and trapped, sure it was the wrong career and ready to look for another job.

qa.q: What made the difference, and what else was sensible in Hansa's advice?
qa.a: Drinking water regularly eased the headaches and the grey evenings; Hansa also wisely said to see a doctor if the headaches kept coming.

qa.q: How might Hansa have been affected before the change?
qa.a: Hansa was snapped at over the dishes and lived with a flatmate who came home flat and irritable, which was hard to put up with.

grounding: Illustrates a professional drinking only tea and coffee at a desk, blaming the job for headaches and low mood, and a water habit lifting both.

passage: For most of last year I was tired in a way sleep didn't touch. I went to bed early, drank water all day and was still thirsty, still dragging myself through the office. I told myself I was lazy and needed more discipline. I tried cold showers, a new planner, no screens at night. Nothing changed. My sister Shreya noticed me refilling my bottle again and again at her birthday lunch. "Sumit, this isn't willpower," she said. "Please see a doctor." I nearly laughed it off. But I went. The doctor listened, asked a lot of questions and ran some tests. It turned out there was a physical reason, and a plan to manage it. I'm less tired now. I wish I'd stopped guessing sooner.

qa.q: What did Shreya notice at her birthday lunch?
qa.a: Sumit refilling the bottle again and again.

qa.q: How did Sumit feel about the tiredness before seeing the doctor?
qa.a: Sumit felt frustrated and ashamed, blaming it on laziness and a lack of discipline.

qa.q: What was the wise choice, and why?
qa.a: Seeing a doctor instead of trying more tricks, because tiredness and thirst that rest and water do not fix can have a physical cause.

qa.q: How does Shreya see what is happening?
qa.a: She sees that it is not about willpower and is worried enough to ask Sumit plainly to see a doctor.

grounding: Shows someone whose fatigue and constant thirst continue despite rest and drinking choosing to see a doctor instead of blaming willpower.

passage:
Supervisor's note, Accounts team, filed privately.
For several weeks Deepika, usually one of our sharpest people, has seemed worn out. She yawns through morning meetings, keeps a large bottle on her desk and refills it often, and told me she has been sleeping long hours and drinking plenty yet still feels drained. Her work is still careful, but she looks exhausted. Today I asked her for a quiet word. I said I wasn't worried about her output, only about her. She admitted she had been blaming herself for being lazy. I said that when tiredness and thirst keep going despite rest, it is worth checking with a doctor rather than guessing. She agreed and booked an appointment. I have given her the morning off for it and will check in with her next week, only about how she is.
Sarita

qa.q: What did Deepika keep on her desk?
qa.a: A large bottle, which she refills often.

qa.q: How had Deepika been feeling about her tiredness?
qa.a: She felt drained and blamed herself for being lazy.

qa.q: What did Sarita do that helped, and why?
qa.a: Sarita asked privately, focused on Deepika rather than her output, suggested a doctor and gave time off for the appointment, which made getting checked easy.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel after the talk?
qa.a: She might feel relieved and less ashamed, knowing her supervisor cared about her rather than just her work.

grounding: Illustrates tiredness and thirst that continue despite rest and drinking being checked by a doctor instead of pushed through with willpower.

passage: Akash, not yet two, was usually all smiles. On Saturday in their Lucknow flat, he woke from his nap screaming. He pushed away his banana, clung to Avni's neck and kept rubbing one ear against her shoulder. That night he kept waking, crying whenever she laid him down. Avni sat up rocking him, watching his fist go back to that ear. "Something hurts, doesn't it?" she whispered. Next morning she took him to the paediatrician down the road.

qa.q: What did Akash push away?
qa.a: His banana.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling when he clung to Avni and rubbed his ear?
qa.a: He was in pain and frightened, and could only show it by crying, clinging and rubbing the ear.

qa.q: What did Avni do well in reading the signs?
qa.a: She noticed the sudden change in mood and the hand going back to his ear, guessed something hurt and took him to the paediatrician.

qa.q: What was the night like for Avni?
qa.a: Long and worrying; she sat up rocking him while he kept waking.

grounding: Shows a toddler who cannot name an ear pain showing it through crying, refusing food, clinging and broken sleep, with the mood change as the first clue.

passage:
"Zeenat won't eat anything," Sarika said, holding her dripping daughter.
Nani leaned in. "Look at her cheek. Red on one side. And all this drool."
Zeenat wailed and chewed hard on Sarika's thumb.
"Teeth," Nani said.
"She's so clingy. She screamed when I put her down."
"Try the cold teether from the fridge, and lots of cuddles."
Zeenat gnawed the teether, sobbing less.
"If it keeps going or worries you, check with the doctor," Nani said.

qa.q: What did Zeenat chew hard on?
qa.a: Sarika's thumb.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when she screamed at being put down?
qa.a: She was sore and upset from her teeth, so she wanted to be held and felt safer close to Sarika.

qa.q: What helped, and what is the sensible next step if it goes on?
qa.a: A cold teether and cuddles helped; if it keeps going or worries them, checking with the doctor is the sensible step.

qa.q: How does Nani read Zeenat's mood?
qa.a: Nani sees the red cheek and drool and reads the fussing as teething pain rather than bad temper.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler with teething pain who cannot name it refusing food, clinging and crying, the mood change being the first clue.

subtype: Child hiding pain to avoid fuss [Actor]
passage: Last month my back tooth hurt for days, and I didn't tell anyone. I was scared the dentist would give me an injection. So I chewed on one side and said I wasn't hungry. When my sister Sarika asked to play carrom, I shouted, "Leave me alone!" and slammed the door. Ammi found me holding my cheek. "Asif, what's hurting?" I cried and told her. She wasn't angry. She hugged me and took me to the dentist the next day. The dentist explained everything first, and it wasn't as bad as I thought. I said sorry to Sarika.

qa.q: What did Asif shout when Sarika asked to play carrom?
qa.a: "Leave me alone!"

qa.q: Why did Asif keep the toothache secret?
qa.a: Asif was scared the dentist would give an injection, so fear made hiding the pain feel safer.

qa.q: What turned things around, and what could Asif do next time?
qa.a: Telling Ammi, who hugged Asif and arranged the dentist; next time, saying something early would end the pain sooner.

qa.q: How might Sarika have felt when the door slammed?
qa.a: Sarika was probably hurt and confused, not knowing the shouting came from a sore tooth.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild hiding a sore tooth out of fear of injections, with the pain leaking out as withdrawal and temper until an adult helps.

subtype: Child hiding pain to avoid fuss [Actor]
passage:
Class teacher's note, Class Three.
Chaitanya is usually chatty and busy, but for two days he has sat curled at his desk, snapping "I'm fine!" when asked anything. Today he refused to go out at break and pushed his tiffin away. At the end of break I sat beside him and said he wasn't in trouble. He whispered that his tummy had been hurting, but he hadn't told anyone because he didn't want to miss the school trip or make his mother worried. I told him telling a grown-up was the right thing, and that we would sort out the trip together. I took him to the school nurse, then phoned his mother, who came to collect him that afternoon to see their doctor. Noor (class teacher)

qa.q: What did Chaitanya push away?
qa.a: His tiffin.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya worried about when he hid his tummy ache?
qa.a: He was anxious about missing the school trip and about making his mother worried, so he kept the pain to himself.

qa.q: Which of Noor's steps helped most, and why?
qa.a: Sitting with him, saying he was not in trouble and reassuring him about the trip, which made it safe to talk; then the nurse and a call home the same day.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya's mother feel after the call?
qa.a: She would likely be concerned but relieved that the teacher noticed and called, so he could see their doctor that day.

grounding: Illustrates a child hiding a tummy ache to avoid missing a trip or worrying a parent, with the pain showing as withdrawal and short temper.
